In fairness to the young lady, she did not declare outright that she would not; she merely voiced a fervent and emphatic wish to be “blessed” if she would. This courteous, delicate avoidance of the request demonstrated the natural good manners of a young woman who could not bear to cause another creature the anguish of a blunt refusal.

The Jew’s face fell. He turned away from this young lady, whose red dress, green boots, and yellow curl-papers made her attire cheerful, if not magnificent, and addressed the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” said the Jew coaxingly, “and what do you say?”

“That it won’t answer, so there’s no use trying it, Fagin,” Nancy replied.

“What’s that supposed to mean?” demanded Mr. Sikes, looking up sullenly.

“Just what I said, Bill,” answered the lady without agitation.

“Why, you’re the very one to do it,” Mr. Sikes argued. “Nobody round here knows a thing about you.”

“And since I don’t wish them to, either,” Nancy returned with the same composure, “my answer’s much more no than yes, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” said Sikes.

“She won’t, Fagin,” Nancy replied.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” said Sikes.

Mr. Sikes proved correct. By alternating threats with promises and bribes, they finally persuaded the lady to accept the errand. The scruples that deterred her agreeable companion did not, in truth, hold Nancy back. Having lately moved to the vicinity of Field Lane from the distant yet genteel suburb of Ratcliffe, she had less cause to fear recognition by any of her many acquaintances.

Thus, with a fresh white apron fastened over her gown and her curl-papers concealed beneath a straw bonnet, both garments supplied from the Jew’s apparently boundless stores, Miss Nancy made ready to set out.

“One moment, my dear,” the Jew said, bringing out a small covered basket. “Hold this in one hand. It gives a more respectable appearance, my dear.”

“Put a door-key in her other hand, Fagin,” suggested Sikes. “That makes it look proper real and genuine.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, indeed it does,” said the Jew, slipping a large front-door key over the forefinger of the young lady’s right hand. “There! Excellent! Excellent indeed, my dear!” he added, rubbing his hands together.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, darling, sweet, innocent little brother!” Nancy cried, breaking into tears and twisting the basket and the door-key in an agony of grief. “What’s happened to him? Where have they carried him? Oh, take pity and tell me what they’ve done with my dear boy, gentlemen! Please do, gentlemen, if you please, gentlemen!”

He made no mention of the matter, however, until their visitor departed for the evening. The moment he was gone, he turned toward his daughter and said:

“Jane, accept my congratulations. You are going to be a very happy woman.”

Jane immediately approached him, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness.

“You are a good girl,” he answered, “and it gives me great satisfaction to think of you so happily established. I have no doubt that you will suit each other wonderfully. Your dispositions are very much alike. You are both so obliging that no decision will ever be reached; so easygoing that every servant will rob you; and so openhanded that you will continually spend beyond your income.”

“I hope that will not happen. Carelessness or a lack of prudence about money would be inexcusable in me.”

“Beyond their income! My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife exclaimed, “what can you mean? He has four or five thousand a year, and quite probably more.” Then she turned to her daughter. “Oh, my darling, darling Jane, how happy I am! I am certain I shall not sleep a wink tonight. I knew this would happen. I always said it must end this way. Surely you could not be so lovely for no purpose! I remember thinking, the very first time I saw him when he arrived in Hertfordshire last year, how likely you were to marry. Oh, he is the handsomest young man anyone ever saw!”

Wickham and Lydia vanished from her thoughts. Jane was now her favorite child beyond all rivalry. At that instant she cared for nobody else. Her younger daughters soon sought Jane’s favor for pleasures she might later have it in her power to grant.

Mary requested access to Netherfield’s library, while Kitty pleaded earnestly for several balls there each winter.

From then onward Bingley naturally visited Longbourn every day, often arriving before breakfast and invariably staying beyond supper, except when some savage neighbor, deserving unlimited hatred, invited him to dinner and he felt bound to accept.

Elizabeth now had few opportunities to talk with her sister, for while Bingley was there Jane could spare attention for no one else. Nevertheless, she discovered that she could be highly useful to both during their inevitable occasional separations. Whenever Jane was absent, he sought Elizabeth’s company for the pleasure of discussing her; and whenever Bingley left, Jane regularly turned to the same source of comfort.

“He has made me so happy,” she said one evening, “by explaining that he had no idea at all I was in town last spring!”

Emma Woodhouse was attractive, intelligent, and wealthy, with a comfortable home and a cheerful nature. She seemed to enjoy some of the finest advantages life could offer, and had reached nearly twenty-one with very little to upset or trouble her.

She was the younger of two daughters of an exceptionally loving, indulgent father. Her sister’s marriage had made her the woman in charge of his household at an early age. Her mother had died so long ago that she retained only a faint memory of her affection. An excellent governess had taken her place and loved Emma almost as a mother would.

Miss Taylor had spent sixteen years with Mr. Woodhouse’s family, more as a friend than a governess. She loved both daughters dearly, but Emma most of all. Their relationship resembled the closeness of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor had ceased to be a governess in name, her gentle disposition had scarcely permitted her to enforce any restrictions. Now that even this trace of authority had long disappeared, they lived together as deeply attached friends. Emma did precisely as she pleased, holding Miss Taylor’s judgment in high regard but following her own for the most part.

Indeed, the real drawbacks to Emma’s circumstances were that she had rather too much power to get her own way and tended to think a little too highly of herself. These were the disadvantages that threatened to spoil her many pleasures. For now, however, she was so unaware of their danger that she did not consider them misfortunes at all.

Sadness came—a mild sadness—but it brought no unpleasant self-awareness. Miss Taylor married. Losing Miss Taylor was Emma’s first experience of grief. On this beloved friend’s wedding day, Emma sat absorbed in sorrow for the first prolonged stretch of her life. When the wedding was over and the wedding party had gone, she and her father were left to dine alone, with no third person expected to enliven the long evening. After dinner her father settled down to sleep as usual, leaving her with nothing to do but reflect on her loss.

The marriage promised every happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston had a faultless character, a comfortable income, a suitable age, and agreeable manners. Emma could take some satisfaction in remembering the generous, selfless friendship with which she had always wished for and encouraged the match. Still, that morning’s business had been a dark one for her. She would miss Miss Taylor every hour of every day. She recalled all her past kindness—the affection and care of sixteen years—how she had taught her and played with her since she was five, how she had devoted every effort to winning her love and amusing her when she was well, and how she had nursed her through the illnesses of childhood.
